question: Subsequent proposals to extend the EU ETS are justified by analyses from climate organisations that downplay the economic and social risks to the European aviation sector. The International Council on Clean Transportation argues that including flights between the EU and third countries in the scheme will induce passengers to choose routes via transfer airports outside the EU to a minimal degree.

On this basis, it concludes that the risk of European airlines and airports losing traffic should not prevent the extension of the ETS. European carriers and trade unions, however, warn of a shift in traffic to hubs in third countries, job losses and a further weakening of the competitiveness of the EU’s aviation sector.

NGOs may participate in the public debate, but they lack a democratic mandate and bear no responsibility for the consequences of the rules that they propose. Their models, assumptions and financial interests cannot replace the Commission’s independent and comprehensive impact assessment. In light of the above: 1.
Is the Commission considering extending the ETS to international flights without first carrying out a full assessment of the impact on European airlines, airports and employment?
Will the Commission review the funding and potential conflicts of interest of the organisations whose analyses it uses when preparing such changes?
Why would the Commission seek to increase the cost of flights from the EU, risking a shift of passengers and traffic to hubs outside the Union?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (2.10.2026)

On 17 July 2026, the Commission adopted its proposal for the revision of the Directive on the EU Emissions Trading System1 (ETS). It includes the extension of the ETS geographical scope to emissions from flights from airports in the European Economic Area (EEA) landing in third country airports located within 5,000 km of the largest aerodrome in the geographical centre of the EU.

All parts of the proposal are based on a rigorous impact assessment2 in line with rules in force for policy-making and legal drafting. The impact assessment was published on the same day as the legislative proposal. It includes impacts on airports, airlines and employment.

According to the above-mentioned assessment, the Commission’s proposal is expected to cause a minor increase in plane ticket prices, while financing a strengthened support to decarbonise the sector and addressing a larger share of EU aviation’s climate impact. The extension also helps mitigating the risk of shift to non-EEA hubs, which may be caused by a variety of factors, beyond climate policies like the ETS.

In its work, the Commission takes into account the input and feedback of a broad range of stakeholders. This includes Member States and competent authorities, industry associations, companies, civil society organisations (including non-governmental organisations), and other interested parties.
A public consultation on the revision of the ETS Directive took place last year, providing all stakeholders with the opportunity to express their views.
